summary.text: A reaction rate is how fast a chemical reaction happens, measured by how quickly a product's concentration rises or a reactant's falls.
Rates vary enormously: iron rusting in air can take many years, while cellulose burning in a fire takes a fraction of a second.
Concentration, pressure, temperature, a catalyst and surface area are among the factors that change how fast a reaction goes.

items.prompt: A pile of coal sits in a room full of air and nothing happens. Someone holds a lit match to it, and it catches and keeps itself hot. What did the match do?

options.label: It added fresh oxygen to the coal, which had been missing from the room before
It raised the temperature enough to get the reaction going, and the reaction then kept heating itself
It turned the coal into a different substance that burns more easily
It switched off the rate, so the coal could finally start to react

items.explain: At room temperature the rate is negligible. The match's heat lets the reaction start, and because it gives off heat it then heats itself.

items.prompt: You double the amount of a reactant crammed into the same flask. Why does the reaction tend to go faster?

options.label: The extra reactant makes the flask hotter, and the heat alone does all the work
Each particle becomes more reactive when it has more neighbours
The extra reactant gets used up first, which clears the way for the rest
The reactant particles meet each other more often, so more collisions happen

items.explain: More concentration means a higher frequency of collisions, which raises the rate.

items.prompt: A cook pours water into a pot of salty water. The salt concentration drops. Has a chemical reaction taken place?

options.label: No, the concentration fell through dilution, with no reaction involved
Yes, any fall in concentration means the salt was used up in a reaction
Yes, because adding a liquid always starts a reaction
Only if the pot is heated, since reactions need heat to show up

items.explain: A concentration can fall with no chemical reaction at all, so the rate definition only applies to a single reaction in a closed system of constant volume.

items.prompt: A reactant's concentration is steadily falling, yet the reaction's rate is always quoted as a positive number. Why?

options.label: The rate measures only the products, which never fall in concentration
Chemists ignore any reactant whose concentration decreases
A minus sign is built into the definition to cancel the fall, leaving a positive rate
The rate is the same as the concentration, so it cannot go down

items.explain: The rate of a reaction is always positive. The negative sign in the formula is there to show the reactant concentration is decreasing.

items.prompt: In a reaction, reactant B is used up three times faster than reactant A. Does the defined reaction rate change depending on whether you track A or B?

options.label: Yes, tracking B always gives a rate three times higher
No, dividing by each substance's stoichiometric number gives the same rate either way
Yes, you must always track the slowest-consumed substance to be correct
No, but only if the reaction takes place in a gas rather than a solution

items.explain: The stoichiometric numbers are included so the defined rate does not depend on which species is measured.

paragraphs.heading: How fast a reaction goes
paragraphs.text: A reaction rate is the speed of a chemical reaction. It is tied to how quickly a product's concentration rises, or a reactant's concentration drops, over each unit of time. Chemists find it by tracking those concentration changes as time passes. The rate always comes out as a positive number, and it is given in units of mol/(L⋅s).

paragraphs.heading: From years to fractions of a second
paragraphs.text: Rates differ enormously from one reaction to the next. Iron rusting in ordinary air is slow and can go on for many years, while cellulose burning in a fire is over in fractions of a second. Some reactions are simply quicker than others by their nature. For most reactions, the pace also slows down as the reaction goes on.

paragraphs.heading: One rate, whatever you measure
paragraphs.text: The ingredients of one reaction can be used up at different speeds. If A has a coefficient of 1 in the equation and B has a coefficient of 3, B disappears three times as fast as A. To get a single rate, each change is scaled by the reciprocal of that substance's stoichiometric number, its count in the equation. That way the rate is the same whichever reactant or product a chemist chooses to watch.

paragraphs.heading: A catch in the definition
paragraphs.text: This simple definition only works for one reaction in a closed system whose volume stays fixed. Concentration can shift for reasons that have nothing to do with chemistry. Pour plain water into a pot of salty water and the salt concentration falls, even though nothing has reacted.

paragraphs.heading: What speeds it up
paragraphs.text: Many things change a reaction's rate, among them the kind of reaction, concentration, pressure, temperature, the solvent, electromagnetic radiation, a catalyst, surface area and stirring. Raising the concentration of a reactant makes its particles collide more often, and the rate rises. For a gas, raising the pressure has the same effect, since it really amounts to raising the gas's concentration.

paragraphs.heading: The role of heat
paragraphs.text: Running a reaction hotter usually makes it faster, partly because particles collide more often. The bigger reason is that more of the colliding particles carry enough energy to react, called the activation energy, so more collisions succeed. The Arrhenius equation describes how temperature affects rate. Not every reaction obeys this pattern: some rates do not change with temperature, and some even fall as it rises.

paragraphs.heading: Why coal needs a match
paragraphs.text: Coal burns in a fireplace where oxygen is around, yet coal kept in storage at room temperature does not. At room temperature the reaction runs so slowly that it is negligible. The heat from a match lets it get going, and after that the reaction warms itself because it releases heat. Other fuels, such as methane, butane and hydrogen, behave the same way.
